title: What is Fascia?
author: Patricia Parkinson
excerpt: Fascia is connective tissue that surrounds, penetrates and connects every part of the body.
body:
Fascia is a type of connective tissue that surrounds, penetrates and connects every part of the body, including bones, muscles, blood vessels and internal organs. It holds the shape of our bodies and affects the body’s balance, strength, and flexibility. It is the conductor of information and wholistic intelligence within us.

Fascia is the organ of shape responsible for maintaining form in gravity. As such, it is richly innervated with mechanoreceptors as reported by Robert Schleip (2003).

Fascia is alive: it senses, it has complex fluid dynamics, and it moves. Fascia organizes the person in gravity as best it can given the individual’s life experiences and genetics.

The first layer of fascia lies under the surface of the skin (superficial fascia). As the fascia gets deeper, it changes in density, wrapping around muscles, bones, tendons and ligaments. Its elasticity, plasticity and resiliency gives it the ability to hold shape and yet still be pliable. When the matrix of fascia is twisted or shortened, it pulls on surrounding structures thereby causing imbalance in the body. This imbalance can be experienced as pain, tightness, or “stress”.

The quality and organization of connective tissue change in accordance to overall lifestyle, physiological responses to stress, exercise, patterns of posture, movement, and accidents.

Everyone on this planet is dealing with the gravitational field. Rolfers use gravity as a tool to direct body organization so “gravity can flow through it” (Dr. Ida P. Rolf).

To do this, Rolfing Structural Integration uses pressure to lengthen and direct the connective tissue to a more efficient place along the body’s line of verticality. Once the body is freed from fascial restriction, it feels light and balanced and can move freely and easily.

title: What are Patterns in the Body?
author: Selena La Brooy
excerpt: Habitual movements and our sense of self create movement memories in the body.
body:
Habitual movements and our sense of self create movement memories (ingrained neural pathways) in the body. The way we choose to use our bodies repetitively actually changes the structure over time.

Any personal trainer will be quick to tell you that repetitive exercises help us sculpt our muscles and bodies. But repetitive movement also trains our physical-psychological habits. If we consider the sheer number of hours we spend in specific movements and positions in our daily lives (sitting in chairs, working, watching TV, texting, gardening, picking up our children, playing sports and so on), it cannot be surprising that these movements and positions cumulatively form our physique and sense of well-being. If we habitually move in unharmonious, misaligned ways, we end up sculpting injury and disease.

The process of Structural Integration includes releasing holding patterns that are contributing to imbalance in the body and introducing new ones that make the body look and feel longer, stronger and more at ease.

Posture or movement patterns can be favourable or not, depending on how well they serve the body’s well-being.

Patterns in the body can be a result of a number of different causes. Some reasons are:

  1. Structural restrictions in the tissues or alignment of skeletal structure (adhesions or layers sticking and not gliding over one another)
  2. Errors in motor coordination.
  3. Habitual pathways as a result of repetitive movements (for work, sports or playing musical instruments, etc.), as a response to protecting the body from injury or anticipated danger (whether real or imagined).

Patterns of imbalance range from subtle to severe and while they may have served the body in the past, they become a hindrance to the body when they are “locked” inside and are unable to release and let go.

For example, when someone has a sprained ankle, the body shifts as much weight as possible onto the uninjured side of the body to protect the injured ankle from further pain. This shift affects how the body stands in gravity and creates an imbalance on one side of the body as it is forced to carry an uneven distribution of weight. As the ankle heals, the body does not automatically shift back from its unbalanced position, for it has learned a new way to cope with injury and a pattern is established.

Contracting in response to pain, holding the breath to block emotions, or slouching to accommodate a computer terminal are examples of patterns that can make the body stiff, rigid, and painful.

Rolfing Structural Integration helps to release places where the tissue may be adhered or stuck and then teaches the body to let go of old ways of holding or moving by introducing new options of movement. This allows the body to experience a sense of physical freedom, strength and moving with ease.

title: What is the Ten Series?
author: Selena La Brooy
excerpt: Over a series of 10 sessions, the practitioner and client work together to let go of poor postural habits and unwind holding patterns.
body:
Over a series of 10 sessions, the practitioner and client work together to let go of poor postural habits and unwind holding patterns that cause the body strain and teach it to move, breathe and live in ways that are balanced, free and upright.

Dr. Rolf developed a systematic approach addressing key areas in each session. While unique to each body, overarching themes include:

Session 1

Opening the surface envelope of the body. Initial assessment of patterns and restrictions affecting breath capacity.

Session 2

Opening the feet and lower leg for mobilization and balance — the foundational platform.

Session 3

Releasing and opening the lateral line of the body.

Session 4

Releasing the mid-line, focusing on medial arch access and pelvic floor.

Session 5

Releasing deeper core, viscera and psoas; retraining functional support for motion.

Session 6

Releasing the backline fascia from eyebrows through head, back, legs to feet. Tension in one area may manifest elsewhere.

Session 7

Releasing and rebalancing head, neck and face fascia, including cranial work through nose and mouth.

Session 8

Organizing and retraining lower limbs to core.

Session 9

Organizing and retraining upper limbs to core.

Session 10

Horizontalizing and achieving whole body balance; anchoring all explorations and retraining.

Sessions may be split or combined with Rolf Movement sessions as needed. Post-series integration typically continues 6–12 months, with additional sessions recommended as life circumstances warrant.

title: What kind of shoes are best for me?
author: Selena La Brooy
excerpt: Options for minimal support maximum mobility footwear.
body:
Many people ask about footwear options. The best shoes offer a wide toe box and maximum mobility for toe and arch movement. Minimal support allows you to strengthen foot muscles rather than rely on built-in arch support. Rigid soles and arch support actually immobilize your feet and weaken intrinsic foot muscles. Good foot health maintains mobility and resilience.

For deeper understanding, Selena recommends biomechanist Katy Bowman’s book Whole Body Barefoot, which explains why minimal shoes work and how to transition safely. Bowman emphasizes: “we cannot go from high support to barefoot shoes or minimal support overnight and not expect injury.” Gradual strengthening is essential.

Recommended Practices

  • Use toe spreaders 20 minutes twice daily while seated or lying down
  • Build foot strength progressively before switching to minimal shoes
  • Visit nutritiousmovement.com for additional resources

Lems, be lenka, vivobarefoot, Groundies, Zaqq, The Drifter Leather, Ahinsa, Feelmax, Vibram FiveFingers

title: What Sitting All Day Does to Your Body
author: Selena La Brooy
excerpt: How prolonged sitting creates specific postural patterns and how Rolfing can help unwind these compensations.
body:
If you work at a desk, you already know the feeling. You start the day sitting up reasonably well, and by mid-afternoon your chin has drifted forward, your shoulders have rounded in, and your lower back aches in a way that has become so familiar you barely notice it. You stand up and everything feels stiff. You stretch, shake it off, and sit back down. The cycle repeats.

What many people do not realize is that prolonged sitting creates very specific structural changes in the body over time. These are not just temporary stiffness. They are patterns that become embedded in the connective tissue, gradually reshaping how the body holds itself even when you are standing and moving.

Let us look at what actually happens. When you sit for extended periods, the hip flexors at the front of the pelvis are held in a shortened position for hours at a time. The fascia in this area adapts by tightening and thickening, pulling the pelvis into an anterior tilt. This places extra load on the lower back, which now has to work harder to keep you upright.

Meanwhile, the head drifts forward to get closer to the screen. For every inch the head moves forward of its ideal position over the spine, the muscles at the back of the neck have to work significantly harder to hold it up. The fascia along the back of the neck and into the upper shoulders thickens and shortens in response. This is one of the most common sources of headaches and neck pain I see in my practice.

The shoulders round forward as the arms reach toward a keyboard or mouse. The pectoral muscles and the fascia across the front of the chest shorten. The upper back muscles become overstretched and weakened. Over months and years, this pattern becomes structural. The body begins to hold this shape not because the muscles are actively contracting, but because the fascial web has reorganized around the pattern.

Here is what I find encouraging. These patterns are not permanent. The fascia is a living, responsive tissue. It shortened and thickened in response to the demands of sitting, and it can be lengthened and reorganized in response to different input. That is precisely what Rolfing does.

In a Rolfing session, we work systematically through the layers of fascia that have adapted to the sitting pattern. We release the shortened hip flexors, open up the front of the chest, restore mobility to the thoracic spine, and bring the head back over the body’s centre of gravity. Clients often describe the sensation of standing after a session as feeling taller, lighter, and more open. They are not imagining it. The structural relationships have genuinely changed.

Of course, Rolfing works best when combined with conscious movement throughout the day. Here are a few simple practices you can start with. Every 30 to 45 minutes, stand up and take a short walk, even if it is just to the kitchen and back. While standing, place your hands on your lower back and gently arch backward a few times to counter the flexed position of sitting. Roll your shoulders back and let your arms hang naturally at your sides for a moment.

Another helpful practice is to sit on the front edge of your chair rather than leaning against the backrest. This engages your core muscles and encourages a more upright posture. It may feel tiring at first, so alternate between this and your usual seated position.

The modern world asks most of us to sit far more than our bodies were designed for. We cannot always change our work circumstances, but we can change how our bodies respond to them. If sitting has left you with chronic tightness, pain, or a posture that does not feel like it belongs to you, Rolfing can help you find your way back to a body that feels balanced and at ease.

title: How Breathing Patterns Affect Your Body
author: Selena La Brooy
excerpt: How restricted breathing creates tension in the ribcage, diaphragm and shoulders, and how Rolfing can help.
body:
Take a moment right now and notice your breathing. Where does the breath move in your body? Does your chest rise and fall? Do your ribs expand to the sides? Does your belly soften and fill? Most of us rarely think about how we breathe, yet our breathing patterns have a profound effect on the way our bodies feel and function every single day.

When we are stressed, anxious, or simply sitting hunched over a screen for hours, our breathing tends to become shallow and confined to the upper chest. Over time, this restricted pattern becomes the norm. The muscles between the ribs, known as the intercostals, lose their flexibility. The diaphragm, that dome-shaped muscle at the base of the ribcage, becomes tight and limited in its range of motion. The accessory breathing muscles in the neck and shoulders pick up the slack, leading to chronic tension in areas that were never designed to be the primary drivers of respiration.

This is where things get interesting from a structural perspective. The fascia surrounding the ribcage, diaphragm, and thoracic spine adapts to these restricted patterns. Connective tissue is incredibly responsive to the demands placed on it. If the ribs rarely expand fully, the fascia around them will gradually shorten and thicken, reinforcing the very pattern that caused the restriction in the first place. It becomes a self-perpetuating cycle.

In my Rolfing practice, I see this pattern frequently. Clients come in with neck pain, shoulder tension, or low back discomfort, and when we begin to explore what is happening structurally, restricted breathing is often a significant contributing factor. The thorax is the centre of the body. When it is locked down, everything above and below has to compensate.

Rolfing addresses this by working directly with the fascial layers around the ribcage and diaphragm. Through careful, sustained pressure, we can encourage the connective tissue to release and lengthen. As the ribs regain their ability to move freely, the diaphragm can descend more fully with each inhalation. Clients often describe the feeling as though they are breathing into parts of their body they had forgotten existed.

The benefits extend well beyond the ribcage. When breathing deepens, the nervous system responds. The parasympathetic branch, responsible for rest and recovery, becomes more active. Stress hormones decrease. Chronic pain patterns that were being amplified by a heightened stress response begin to settle. It is remarkable how much can shift when the body simply has more room to breathe.

There are also things you can explore on your own. Try this simple practice: sit comfortably and place your hands on the sides of your lower ribs. As you inhale, see if you can direct the breath sideways into your hands. You are not trying to force anything. Just invite the ribs to expand laterally. Do this for five or six breaths, a few times throughout the day. You may notice that your shoulders begin to drop, your neck softens, and there is a general sense of ease that was not there before.

Another helpful practice is to lie on your back with your knees bent and simply observe your breathing for a few minutes. Notice what moves and what stays still. Over time, the act of paying attention to the breath can begin to change the pattern on its own. The body is remarkably good at self-correcting when given the right input.

If you find that your breathing feels consistently shallow or effortful, it may be worth exploring what structural factors are contributing. Sometimes all the body needs is a little help releasing the fascial restrictions that have accumulated over years of habitual patterning. That is exactly what Rolfing is designed to do.

title: Your Relationship with Gravity
author: Selena La Brooy
excerpt: Dr. Ida Rolf's core insight: how a well-organized body moves effortlessly with gravity rather than fighting against it.
body:
Gravity is the one force that never takes a day off. From the moment we stand up in the morning until we lie down at night, our bodies are in constant negotiation with the gravitational field. Most of us never think about this relationship, yet it was the central insight behind Dr. Ida Rolf’s life work and the foundation of everything we do in Rolfing Structural Integration.

Dr. Rolf understood something that seems simple but has profound implications. When the major segments of the body, the head, thorax, pelvis, and legs, are well aligned and balanced around a vertical axis, gravity flows through the body like a supportive force. The bones do the work of holding us up, and the muscles are free to do what they do best, which is to create movement. But when these segments are misaligned, shifted forward or back, tilted or rotated, the muscles have to take over the job of holding the body upright. That is exhausting work, and it is the source of much of the chronic pain and fatigue people experience.

Think of it this way. Imagine stacking a set of building blocks perfectly on top of one another. The stack is stable and requires no effort to maintain. Now shift one of the middle blocks slightly to the side. The blocks above it have to compensate, and the whole structure becomes less stable. It takes external support to keep it from toppling. In the body, that external support comes from muscles and fascia that are working overtime, day after day, just to keep you upright.

What does a well-organized body actually feel like? People who have experienced it often describe a sense of length and lift. There is a feeling of being taller without trying, as though the spine is gently lengthening upward. The shoulders rest easily without being held back. The head floats on top of the spine rather than being propped up by tense neck muscles. There is a quality of buoyancy, a sense that gravity is actually supporting you rather than dragging you down.

This is not an abstract ideal. It is something that can be felt and recognized in the body. Many of my clients describe it after their first few Rolfing sessions. They notice that standing feels easier, that walking has a quality of flow that was not there before. Some say they feel lighter, even though nothing about their weight has changed. What has changed is the relationship between their structure and the gravitational field.

The process of Rolfing works toward this by systematically releasing fascial restrictions that are holding the body in patterns of misalignment. Session by session, we work through the layers of the body, addressing the superficial fascia first and then moving deeper into the core structures. The goal is not to force the body into some ideal posture, but to remove the restrictions that are preventing it from finding its own natural balance.

Dr. Rolf famously said, “When the body gets working appropriately, the force of gravity can flow through. Then, spontaneously, the body heals itself.” This was not a mystical statement. It was a practical observation. When the body is well organized in gravity, circulation improves, breathing deepens, the nervous system calms, and the tissues receive better nourishment. The body’s own healing mechanisms function more efficiently when they are not burdened by the constant effort of fighting gravity.

One of the things I love about this work is watching the moment when a client first experiences that sense of effortless uprightness. There is often a look of surprise, as though they had forgotten what it felt like to simply stand without effort. For many people, the experience of being well organized in gravity is something they have not felt since childhood.

Gravity is not the enemy. It is a force that can either work for you or against you, depending on how your body is organized. Rolfing is, at its heart, about changing that relationship so that gravity becomes your ally. When it does, everything changes. Movement becomes easier, pain diminishes, and there is a quality of ease and vitality that permeates daily life.

If you have been carrying the weight of gravity as a burden rather than a support, I invite you to explore what is possible when that relationship shifts.

title: Rolfing for Athletes and Active Bodies
author: Selena La Brooy
excerpt: How athletes and active people benefit from Rolfing through improved range of motion, injury prevention, and recovery.
body:
If you are someone who moves your body regularly, whether you run, hike, climb, practice yoga, or play a sport, you probably already have a good sense of what your body can do. You may also have a growing awareness of where it gets stuck. That persistent tightness in one hip, the shoulder that never quite feels free, the knee that complains on steep descents. These are the kinds of patterns that bring active people to Rolfing.

Every form of movement creates specific demands on the body. Running, for example, is a beautifully repetitive activity. The same muscles fire in the same sequence, stride after stride, kilometre after kilometre. Over time, the fascia adapts to support this particular movement pattern. The tissues that are used most become denser and more defined. But this specialization comes at a cost. Areas that are not being asked to participate become less mobile, and the body gradually loses some of its overall adaptability.

I see this frequently with trail runners and hikers here on Salt Spring Island. The terrain is hilly and varied, which is wonderful for building strength, but the repetitive nature of climbing and descending creates predictable patterns. The calves and hip flexors tighten. The IT band becomes dense and restricted. The ankles lose some of their lateral mobility. None of these changes are injuries in themselves, but they set the stage for injury by reducing the body’s ability to adapt to unexpected demands.

Climbers present a different but equally recognizable pattern. The forearms, shoulders, and lats become extraordinarily strong and developed, while the front of the body may become relatively shortened. The fascial balance between the front and back of the body shifts, and over time this can affect everything from breathing capacity to low back comfort.

Yoga practitioners sometimes come to Rolfing with a different kind of imbalance. They may have excellent flexibility in certain ranges of motion, but the connective tissue has become so elastic in some areas that stability is compromised. Rolfing can help by differentiating the layers of fascia and bringing more organization to the relationships between muscles, so that flexibility is supported by structural integrity.

What Rolfing offers athletes is not just pain relief or recovery, though those are valuable benefits. The deeper gift is improved structural efficiency. When the fascial web is well organized, the body moves with less internal friction. Range of motion increases not because muscles have been stretched, but because the connective tissue is allowing movement to flow through the body more freely. Many athletes report that after a series of Rolfing sessions, their movements feel smoother and more effortless. They can access power they did not know was available.

Recovery is another area where Rolfing makes a real difference. When fascia is restricted, circulation to the surrounding tissues is reduced. Metabolic waste from exercise does not clear as efficiently, and fresh nutrients are slower to arrive. By releasing fascial adhesions and restoring healthy tissue hydration, Rolfing supports the body’s natural recovery processes. Many of my athletic clients schedule sessions during periods of heavy training or after particularly demanding events.

Injury prevention is perhaps the most significant long-term benefit. Most sports injuries do not happen randomly. They happen in areas where the body has been compensating for a structural imbalance. A runner with restricted ankle mobility will eventually place excessive strain on the knee or hip. A climber with a tight thorax will overwork the shoulder. By addressing these imbalances before they become injuries, Rolfing helps active people stay in the activities they love.

If you are active and curious about what Rolfing could do for your performance and longevity in your sport, I would love to have that conversation. Every body tells a unique story, and understanding the patterns your activities have created is the first step toward moving with greater freedom and resilience.
